claim: Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling in mature astrocytes is required for establishing structural organization and remodeling of cortical synapses in a cell type-specific manner.
source: Here, we show that Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling in mature astrocytes is required for establishing structural organization and remodeling of cortical synapses in a cell type-specific manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including spine density measurements, in vivo imaging, and electrophysiology experiments.

claim: In the postnatal cortex, Shh signaling is active in a subpopulation of mature astrocytes localized primarily in deep cortical layers.
source: In the postnatal cortex, Shh signaling is active in a subpopulation of mature astrocytes localized primarily in deep cortical layers.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing Gli1 expression patterns in astrocytes across cortical layers (Figure 1).

claim: Selective disruption of Shh signaling in astrocytes produces a dramatic increase in synapse number specifically on layer V apical dendrites that emerges during adolescence and persists into adulthood.
source: Selective disruption of Shh signaling in astrocytes produces a dramatic increase in synapse number specifically on layer V apical dendrites that emerges during adolescence and persists into adulthood.
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density measurements across developmental time points in Gfap Smo CKO mice (Figure 2).

claim: Dynamic turnover of dendritic spines is impaired in mutant mice.
source: Dynamic turnover of dendritic spines is impaired in mutant mice and is accompanied by an increase in neuronal excitability and a reduction of the glial-specific, inward-rectifying K+ channel Kir4.1.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data showing reduced spine turnover ratios and altered spine dynamics (Figure 3).

claim: Gfap Smo CKO mice show an increase in neuronal excitability.
source: Dynamic turnover of dendritic spines is impaired in mutant mice and is accompanied by an increase in neuronal excitability and a reduction of the glial-specific, inward-rectifying K+ channel Kir4.1.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings showing increased action potential firing (Figure 5).

claim: Gfap Smo CKO mice show a reduction of the glial-specific, inward-rectifying K+ channel Kir4.1.
source: Dynamic turnover of dendritic spines is impaired in mutant mice and is accompanied by an increase in neuronal excitability and a reduction of the glial-specific, inward-rectifying K+ channel Kir4.1.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and ddPCR data showing reduced Kir4.1 expression (Figure 4).

claim: Astrocytes are critical regulators of synaptic connectivity and function.
source: Considerable evidence now shows that, together with neurons, astrocytes are critical regulators of synaptic connectivity and function (Allen and Eroglu, 2017; Adamsky et al., 2018; Risher et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Astrocytes interact intimately with synapses to regulate their formation, maturation, and function.
source: Astrocytes interact intimately with synapses to regulate their formation, maturation, and function, and a growing number of astrocyte-secreted proteins that directly mediate synapse formation and elimination have been identified (Allen et al., 2012; Kucukdereli et al., 2011; Christopherson et al., 2005; Blanco-Suarez et al., 2018; Chung et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Astrocytes regulate concentrations of K+ and glutamate in the extracellular space, thereby modulating neuronal activity.
source: In addition, astrocytes regulate concentrations of K+ and glutamate in the extracellular space, thereby modulating neuronal activity (Olsen and Sontheimer, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The molecular signaling pathway Sonic hedgehog (Shh) governs a broad array of neurodevelopmental processes in the vertebrate embryo, including morphogenesis, cell proliferation and specification, and axon pathfinding.
source: The molecular signaling pathway Sonic hedgehog (Shh) governs a broad array of neurodevelopmental processes in the vertebrate embryo, including morphogenesis, cell proliferation and specification, and axon pathfinding (Fuccillo et al., 2006; Ruiz i Altaba et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Shh activity persists in multiple cell populations in the postnatal and adult CNS, including progenitor cells, as well as in differentiated neurons and astrocytes.
source: However, Shh activity persists in multiple cell populations in the postnatal and adult CNS, including progenitor cells, as well as in differentiated neurons and astrocytes (Traiffort et al., 2010; Ahn and Joyner, 2005; Ihrie et al., 2011; Harwell et al., 2012; Garcia et al., 2010), where novel and unexpected roles for Shh activity are emerging (Garcia et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Following injury, Shh has been shown to mitigate inflammation.
source: Following injury, Shh has been shown to mitigate inflammation (Alvarez et al., 2011; Allahyari et al., 2019), and in the cerebellum, Shh derived from Purkinje neurons instructs phenotypic properties of mature Bergmann glia (Farmer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the cerebellum, Shh derived from Purkinje neurons instructs phenotypic properties of mature Bergmann glia.
source: Following injury, Shh has been shown to mitigate inflammation (Alvarez et al., 2011; Allahyari et al., 2019), and in the cerebellum, Shh derived from Purkinje neurons instructs phenotypic properties of mature Bergmann glia (Farmer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the postnatal cortex, Shh is required for establishing local circuits between two distinct projection neuron populations.
source: In the postnatal cortex, Shh is required for establishing local circuits between two distinct projection neuron populations (Harwell et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Shh produced by layer V neurons guides the formation of synaptic connections to its layer II/III presynaptic partners, which transduce the Shh signal through non-canonical, Gli-independent mechanisms.
source: Shh produced by layer V neurons guides the formation of synaptic connections to its layer II/III presynaptic partners, which transduce the Shh signal through non-canonical, Gli-independent mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the cited work (Harwell et al., 2012).

claim: Shh signaling is active in a discrete subpopulation of cortical astrocytes.
source: We have previously shown that Shh signaling is also active in a discrete subpopulation of cortical astrocytes (Garcia et al., 2010), suggesting that Shh signaling mediates both homotypic and heterotypic cellular interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Astrocytes engaging in Shh activity are identified by expression of Gli1, a transcriptional effector of canonical Shh signaling.
source: Astrocytes engaging in Shh activity are identified by expression of Gli1, a transcriptional effector of canonical Shh signaling (Fuccillo et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and established knowledge about Gli1 as a Shh pathway effector.

claim: Dendritic spines are the structural hosts of most excitatory synapses and play an important role in the organization and function of neural circuits.
source: Dendritic spines are the structural hosts of most excitatory synapses and play an important role in the organization and function of neural circuits.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about dendritic spines.

claim: Deep layer neurons exhibit long-lasting aberrations in the density and turnover of dendritic spines that emerge during postnatal development following selective disruption of Shh signaling in astrocytes.
source: We show that deep layer neurons exhibit long-lasting aberrations in the density and turnover of dendritic spines that emerge during postnatal development following selective disruption of Shh signaling in astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on spine density and dynamics (Figures 2 and 3).

claim: Perturbations in synaptic organization are not observed in upper layer neurons where Gli1 astrocytes are relatively sparse.
source: These perturbations in synaptic organization are not observed in upper layer neurons where Gli1 astrocytes are relatively sparse.
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density measurements in layer II/III neurons (Figure 2).

claim: Chronic in vivo imaging of dendritic spines reveals that mutant mice exhibit lower rates of spine turnover, suggesting impaired structural plasticity.
source: Chronic in vivo imaging of dendritic spines reveals that mutant mice exhibit lower rates of spine turnover, suggesting impaired structural plasticity.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data (Figure 3) and involves inference about structural plasticity.

claim: Gfap Smo CKO mice show a pronounced deficit in expression of the glial-specific inward-rectifying K+ channel, Kir4.1.
source: In addition, these mice show a pronounced deficit in expression of the glial-specific inward-rectifying K+ channel, Kir4.1, as well as an increase in excitability of cortical neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and ddPCR data (Figure 4).

claim: Gfap Smo CKO mice show an increase in excitability of cortical neurons.
source: In addition, these mice show a pronounced deficit in expression of the glial-specific inward-rectifying K+ channel, Kir4.1, as well as an increase in excitability of cortical neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 5).

claim: Astrocytes act as key modulators of neural activity and structure during postnatal development in a Shh-dependent manner.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that astrocytes act as key modulators of neural activity and structure during postnatal development in a Shh-dependent manner and further establish Shh signaling as a fundamental mediator of synaptic connectivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 44% of astrocytes in layer IV express Gli1.
source: This analysis showed that 44% of astrocytes in layer IV express Gli1 (Figure 1), while 36% of astrocytes in layer V express Gli1.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Gli1 expression in astrocytes shown in Figure 1.

claim: 36% of astrocytes in layer V express Gli1.
source: This analysis showed that 44% of astrocytes in layer IV express Gli1 (Figure 1), while 36% of astrocytes in layer V express Gli1.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Gli1 expression in astrocytes shown in Figure 1.

claim: The distribution of Gli1 astrocytes in layer V was not homogenous, showing an enrichment of marked cells in layer Vb, and a distinctive paucity of marked cells in layer Va.
source: Interestingly, the distribution of Gli1 astrocytes in layer V was not homogenous, showing an enrichment of marked cells in layer Vb, and a distinctive paucity of marked cells in layer Va (Figure 1), consistent with the localization of Shh producing neurons in layer Vb (Harwell et al., 2012; Garcia et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: 75% of marked cells were found in layer Vb whereas only 25% were found in layer Va.
source: We analyzed the fraction of Gli1 astrocytes in each sublayer of layer V and found that 75% of marked cells were found in layer Vb whereas only 25% were found in layer Va.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Gli1 astrocyte distribution in layer V sublayers.

claim: Layers II/III and VI showed the lowest fractions of marked astrocytes, with only 11% and 22% of S100β cells expressing tomato, respectively.
source: Layers II/III and VI showed the lowest fractions of marked astrocytes, with only 11% and 22% of S100β cells expressing tomato, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Gli1 expression in astrocytes across cortical layers.

claim: Gli1 astrocytes are preferentially localized in deep cortical layers.
source: These data demonstrate that Gli1 astrocytes are preferentially localized in deep cortical layers and suggest their interactions with local neurons may differ from that of Gli1-negative astrocytes in superficial layers.
evidence: The claim is supported by the laminar distribution data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The interactions of Gli1 astrocytes with local neurons may differ from that of Gli1-negative astrocytes in superficial layers.
source: These data demonstrate that Gli1 astrocytes are preferentially localized in deep cortical layers and suggest their interactions with local neurons may differ from that of Gli1-negative astrocytes in superficial layers.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed laminar distribution of Gli1 astrocytes.

claim: Transduction of canonical Shh signaling begins with binding of Shh to its transmembrane receptor, Patched1 (Ptch), relieving inhibition of a second, obligatory co-receptor Smoothened (Smo).
source: Transduction of canonical Shh signaling begins with binding of Shh to its transmembrane receptor, Patched1 (Ptch), relieving inhibition of a second, obligatory co-receptor Smoothened (Smo).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of the Shh signaling pathway.

claim: Gfap-Cre transgenic mice have Cre expression regulated by the full-length mouse Gfap promoter.
source: To investigate the role of Shh signaling in astrocyte function, we performed conditional knockout of Smo selectively in astrocytes using Gfap-Cre transgenic mice in which Cre expression is regulated by the full-length mouse Gfap promoter (Garcia et al., 2004) (Gfap Smo CKO).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the original description of the mouse line.

claim: Gfap-mediated Cre recombination targets astrocyte progenitors expressing GFAP which are present at birth.
source: Because Gfap-mediated Cre recombination targets astrocyte progenitors expressing GFAP which are present at birth, this is an effective tool for targeting the cortical astrocyte population for selective gene deletion.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of GFAP expression during development and the timing of Cre activity.

claim: The vast majority of tomato-positive cells showed a bushy morphology, typical of protoplasmic astrocytes.
source: The vast majority of tomato-positive cells showed a bushy morphology, typical of protoplasmic astrocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nearly 70% of tomato-positive cells were co-labeled with S100β, identifying them as astrocytes.
source: Single cell analysis of double staining with S100β showed that nearly 70% were co-labeled, identifying them as astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A small fraction (6%) of tomato cells was identified as oligodendrocytes.
source: We also identified a small fraction (6%) of tomato cells as oligodendrocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A small fraction (9%) of tomato cells were co-labeled with the neuronal marker, NeuN, but this represented only 1.3% of cortical neurons.
source: A small fraction (9%) of tomato cells were co-labeled with the neuronal marker, NeuN, but this represented only 1.3% of cortical neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nearly all cortical astrocytes analyzed expressed the tdTomato reporter protein (95%).
source: Importantly, although a minor fraction of recombined cells was identified as neurons or oligodendrocytes, nearly all cortical astrocytes analyzed expressed the tdTomato reporter protein (95%; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting effective targeting of the cortical astrocyte population using this Gfap-Cre driver.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gfap Smo CKO mice show a 50% reduction in the number of Smo transcripts.
source: We performed qPCR on whole cortex from Gfap Smo CKO mice and littermate controls and found a 50% reduction in the number of Smo transcripts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The remaining Smo transcripts in Gfap Smo CKO mice are likely due to neurons that do not undergo Cre-mediated recombination.
source: As Smo is also expressed in neurons (Harwell et al., 2012), the remaining Smo transcripts are likely due to neurons that do not undergo Cre-mediated recombination in these mice.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the qPCR data and knowledge that Smo is expressed in neurons.

claim: Gfap Smo CKO mice show a nearly complete loss of Gli1 activity.
source: Importantly, Gfap Smo CKO mice show a nearly complete loss of Gli1 activity, with no difference in the number of astrocytes in the mature cortex, demonstrating effective interruption of canonical Shh signaling (Garcia et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: There is no difference in the number of astrocytes in the mature cortex of Gfap Smo CKO mice.
source: Importantly, Gfap Smo CKO mice show a nearly complete loss of Gli1 activity, with no difference in the number of astrocytes in the mature cortex, demonstrating effective interruption of canonical Shh signaling (Garcia et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: During postnatal development, Shh is required for establishing synaptic connectivity between layer V neurons and their presynaptic partners in layer II/III, which is mediated by Gli-independent, non-canonical signaling.
source: During postnatal development, Shh is required for establishing synaptic connectivity between layer V neurons and their presynaptic partners in layer II/III, which is mediated by Gli-independent, non-canonical signaling (Harwell et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Dendritic spines receive the vast majority of excitatory input, thereby serving as a useful readout of synaptic connectivity.
source: Dendritic spines receive the vast majority of excitatory input, thereby serving as a useful readout of synaptic connectivity (Nimchinsky et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: Dendritic spines undergo a period of dynamic reorganization during postnatal development during which there is an initial overproduction of spines over the first 2–3 weeks of postnatal development followed by a period of synaptic pruning that refines the precise connectivity of cortical circuits.
source: Dendritic spines undergo a period of dynamic reorganization during postnatal development during which there is an initial overproduction of spines over the first 2–3 weeks of postnatal development followed by a period of synaptic pruning that refines the precise connectivity of cortical circuits (Zuo et al., 2005a).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: At P14, spine density was comparable between Gfap Smo CKO mice and wild type littermate controls.
source: At P14, spine density was comparable between Gfap Smo CKO mice and wild type (WT) littermate controls, suggesting that early synaptogenesis does not require astrocytic Shh signaling (0.58 ± 0.03 spines/µm and 0.56 ± 0.01 spines/µm, WT [n = 7 cells] and Gfap Smo CKO [n = 6 cells], respectively, p=0.64, two animals per genotype).
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density measurements at P14.

claim: Early synaptogenesis does not require astrocytic Shh signaling.
source: At P14, spine density was comparable between Gfap Smo CKO mice and wild type (WT) littermate controls, suggesting that early synaptogenesis does not require astrocytic Shh signaling (0.58 ± 0.03 spines/µm and 0.56 ± 0.01 spines/µm, WT [n = 7 cells] and Gfap Smo CKO [n = 6 cells], respectively, p=0.64, two animals per genotype).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparable spine density at P14.

claim: Between P14 and P21, spine density remained stable in WT.
source: Between P14 and P21, spine density remained stable in WT, but showed a dramatic increase at P28 (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Spine density showed a dramatic increase at P28 in WT mice.
source: Between P14 and P21, spine density remained stable in WT, but showed a dramatic increase at P28 (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: This period of synapse addition was followed by a steady reduction in spine density at P42 and into adulthood (≥P90) in WT mice, reflecting the developmental elimination of spines.
source: This period of synapse addition was followed by a steady reduction in spine density at P42 and into adulthood (≥P90), reflecting the developmental elimination of spines.
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density measurements across developmental time points and involves inference about developmental processes.

claim: Gfap Smo CKO mice showed an accelerated timeline of spine addition in which spine density increased dramatically between P14 and P21.
source: In contrast, Gfap Smo CKO mice showed an accelerated timeline of spine addition in which spine density increased dramatically between P14 and P21 (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Spine density was significantly higher at P21 in Gfap Smo CKO mice compared to controls.
source: Spine density was significantly higher at P21 in Gfap Smo CKO mice compared to controls (0.53 ± 0.05 spines/µm and 0.76 ± 0.06 spines/µm, WT [n = 9 cells] and Gfap Smo CKO [n = 9 cells], respectively, p=0.008, three animals per genotype).
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density measurements at P21.

claim: Spine density remained elevated in adult Gfap Smo CKO mice compared to WT controls.
source: Although there was a modest reduction in spine density as animals matured, spine density remained elevated in adult Gfap Smo CKO mice compared to WT controls (0.36 ± 0.02 spines/µm and 0.60 ± 0.02 spines/µm in WT [n = 24 cells] and Gfap Smo CKO [n = 23 cells], respectively, p<0.0001, four animals per genotype; Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density measurements in adult mice shown in Figure 2.

claim: WT mice experience a 49% reduction in spine density from the peak of spine density at P28 to adulthood.
source: Thus, whereas WT mice experience a 49% reduction in spine density from the peak of spine density at P28 to adulthood, Gfap Smo CKO mice exhibit a 22% reduction from their peak at P21 to adulthood.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from the spine density measurements.

claim: Gfap Smo CKO mice exhibit a 22% reduction in spine density from their peak at P21 to adulthood.
source: Thus, whereas WT mice experience a 49% reduction in spine density from the peak of spine density at P28 to adulthood, Gfap Smo CKO mice exhibit a 22% reduction from their peak at P21 to adulthood.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from the spine density measurements.

claim: There is no difference in basal dendrite spine density in Gfap Smo CKO mice.
source: Interestingly, we find no difference in basal dendrite spine density in Gfap Smo CKO mice (0.60 ± 0.04 spines/um and 0.62 ± 0.04 spines/µm in WT [n = 10 cells] and Gfap Smo CKO [n = 10 cells], respectively, p=0.71, three animals per genotype; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density measurements of basal dendrites shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Embryonic deletion of Shh from neurons using the Emx-Cre driver produces a reduction in spine density of basal dendrites on layer V neurons.
source: This is in contrast to embryonic deletion of Shh from neurons using the Emx-Cre driver, which produces a reduction in spine density of basal dendrites on layer V neurons (Harwell et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: While the early stages of synapse formation proceed independently of astrocytic Shh signaling, the maturing cortical circuit requires intact Shh activity in astrocytes for the developmental pruning of excess synapses necessary to achieve its mature organization.
source: These data suggest that while the early stages of synapse formation proceed independently of astrocytic Shh signaling, the maturing cortical circuit requires intact Shh activity in astrocytes for the developmental pruning of excess synapses necessary to achieve its mature organization.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the developmental spine density data.

claim: Pyramidal neurons in layer II/III of WT mice showed a higher spine density than layer V neurons.
source: Pyramidal neurons in layer II/III of WT mice showed a higher spine density than layer V neurons (0.79 ± 0.06 spines/µm, n = 7 cells, four animals) consistent with previous studies (Holtmaat et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density measurements and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Layer II/III spine density was not significantly different between WT and Gfap Smo CKO mice.
source: However, this was not significantly different from the spine density observed in Gfap Smo CKO mice (0.76 ± 0.06 spines/µm, p=0.76, n = 9 cells, five animals; Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mature, differentiated astrocytes expressing Gli1 are relatively sparse in the hippocampus.
source: Although the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus harbors a population of Gli1-expressing adult neural progenitor cells, mature, differentiated astrocytes expressing Gli1 are relatively sparse (Ahn and Joyner, 2005; Han et al., 2008) (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature and data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The spine density of CA1 pyramidal neurons in adult mice was higher than in cortical neurons.
source: The spine density of CA1 pyramidal neurons in adult mice was higher than in cortical neurons, consistent with previous studies (Attardo et al., 2015; Perez-Cruz et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density measurements and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: There was no significant difference in CA1 spine density between Gfap Smo CKO mice and WT controls.
source: However, there was no significant difference in spine density between Gfap Smo CKO mice and WT controls (0.97 ± 0.05 spines/µm and 0.90 ± 0.05 spines/µm in WT [n = 11 cells] and Gfap Smo CKO [n = 11 cells], respectively, p=0.32, three animals per genotype; Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Some cortical neurons undergo recombination in Gfap-Cre mice.
source: Our analysis of the recombination pattern of the Gfap-Cre driver showed that some cortical neurons undergo recombination (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Smo deletion in a small population of neurons is not responsible for the elevated spine density of layer V neurons.
source: To rule out the possibility that Smo deletion in a small population of neurons is responsible for the elevated spine density of layer V neurons, we deleted Smo in excitatory neurons using the CamKIIα-Cre driver (CK2 Smo CKO), and evaluated spine density of layer V neurons in adult mice.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental design to test this possibility.

claim: There was no significant difference in spine density between CK2 Smo CKO mice and littermate controls.
source: We found no significant difference in spine density between CK2 Smo CKO mice and littermate controls (0.77 ± 0.07 spines/µm and 0.59 ± 0.06 spines/µm in WT [n = 10 cells] and CK2 Smo CKO [n = 9 cells], respectively, p=0.07, three animals per genotype; Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Shh activity in astrocytes is necessary for the developmental reorganization of dendritic spines specifically on layer V cortical neurons.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Shh activity in astrocytes is necessary for the developmental reorganization of dendritic spines specifically on layer V cortical neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data.

claim: Elevated spine density was observed along the apical dendrites of layer V neurons, which traverse layer II/III, where few Gli1 astrocytes are found.
source: Notably, we observed elevated spine density along the apical dendrites of layer V neurons, which traverse layer II/III, where few Gli1 astrocytes are found.
evidence: The claim is supported by the spine density data and the laminar distribution of Gli1 astrocytes.

claim: The modification of synapse organization mediated by Gli1 astrocytes does not occur through direct astrocyte-synapse interactions.
source: This suggests that the modification of synapse organization mediated by Gli1 astrocytes does not occur through direct astrocyte-synapse interactions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that elevated spine density occurs in regions with few Gli1 astrocytes.

claim: Dendritic spines are dynamic structures that undergo rapid formation and elimination during postnatal cortical development.
source: Dendritic spines are dynamic structures that undergo rapid formation and elimination during postnatal cortical development.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about spine dynamics.

claim: As cortical circuits mature, the fraction of spines undergoing dynamic turnover declines concomitant with an increase in spine stability.
source: As cortical circuits mature, the fraction of spines undergoing dynamic turnover declines concomitant with an increase in spine stability (Zuo et al., 2005a; Holtmaat et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The dynamic turnover of spines has long been considered a structural correlate of synaptic plasticity and can be regulated in an activity-dependent manner.
source: The dynamic turnover of spines has long been considered a structural correlate of synaptic plasticity and can be regulated in an activity-dependent manner (Lendvai et al., 2000; Trachtenberg et al., 2002; Holtmaat and Svoboda, 2009; Zuo et al., 2005b).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: In WT mice, the turnover ratio was 0.14 at P17-P21 and 0.10 in P28-P32 mice.
source: In WT mice, the turnover ratio was 0.14 at P17-P21 (n = 5 mice) and 0.10 in P28-P32 mice (n = 3 mice; Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by spine turnover measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: In Gfap Smo CKO mice, the turnover ratio was lower at P17-P21 than in WT mice, and remained stable at P28-P32.
source: In Gfap Smo CKO mice however, the turnover ratio was lower at P17-P21 than in WT mice, and remained stable at P28-P32 (0.11 and 0.10, respectively, n = 4 mice; Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by spine turnover measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: Dendritic spines in Gfap Smo CKO mice stabilize earlier than those in WT mice.
source: This suggests that dendritic spines in Gfap Smo CKO mice stabilize earlier than those in WT mice.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the turnover ratio data.

claim: The fraction of filopodia was lower in juvenile Gfap Smo CKO mice compared to WT controls.
source: Consistent with this, we found that the fraction of filopodia was lower in juvenile Gfap Smo CKO mice compared to WT controls (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by filopodia fraction measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: Filopodia are structural precursors of dendritic spines and exhibit higher rates of dynamic turnover than mature spines.
source: Filopodia are structural precursors of dendritic spines and exhibit higher rates of dynamic turnover than mature spines (Ziv and Smith, 1996; Berry and Nedivi, 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The density of filopodia declines as the cortex matures.
source: Accordingly, the density of filopodia declines as the cortex matures (Zuo et al., 2005a; Grutzendler et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The fraction of all protrusions in juvenile WT mice identified as filopodia was 25%, but that fraction declined significantly to 15% in adults.
source: Indeed, the fraction of all protrusions in juvenile WT mice (n = 7 mice) identified as filopodia was 25%, but that fraction declined significantly to 15% in adults (n = 16 mice, p=0.0039; Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by filopodia fraction measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was no age-dependent decline in filopodia fraction in Gfap Smo CKO mice.
source: In contrast, we did not observe this age-dependent decline in Gfap Smo CKO mice (17% and 12% in juvenile [n = 10 mice] and adult [n = 7 mice] Gfap Smo CKO mice, respectively, p=0.398).
evidence: The claim is supported by filopodia fraction measurements.

claim: The filopodial fraction in juvenile Gfap Smo CKO mice was significantly below WT levels and comparable to adult WT levels.
source: The filopodial fraction in juvenile Gfap Smo CKO mice was already significantly below WT levels and comparable to adult WT levels, suggesting that nascent spines undergo accelerated stabilization in the absence of astrocyte-mediated Shh signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by filopodia fraction measurements and involves inference about spine stabilization.

claim: Nascent spines undergo accelerated stabilization in the absence of astrocyte-mediated Shh signaling.
source: The filopodial fraction in juvenile Gfap Smo CKO mice was already significantly below WT levels and comparable to adult WT levels, suggesting that nascent spines undergo accelerated stabilization in the absence of astrocyte-mediated Shh signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the filopodia fraction data.

claim: In P17-21 mice, WT and CKO mice showed similar proportions of mature spines (54% and 55% in WT and CKO, respectively).
source: In P17-21 mice, WT and CKO mice showed similar proportions of mature spines (54% and 55% in WT and CKO, respectively, n = 4 mice per genotype; Figure 3), however Gfap Smo CKO mice showed an apparent increase in protrusions with an intermediate morphology (16% and 26% in WT and CKO, respectively; Figure 3), though this was not statistically significant.
